reviews.desc: Outer Heaven is a little club on the Lower East Side where you can dance to electronic music, get bottle service, and play a few vintage arcade games.
reviews.text: let us help you make a decision Outer Heaven 191 Chrystie St, New York, NY 10002 Outer Heaven describes itself as a “microclub,” which is exactly what it sounds like (an especially small club). Geared toward dancing, this little spot on the Lower East Side plays house, disco, and techno through a sound system designed by the founder of Cielo and Output. The space has a minimalist Japandi-style interior, and it’s divided into two small rooms: a bar with a subtle anime theme and a dance floor with a DJ booth. There are also a few arcade games tucked to the side, and you'll find a comic book stand at the entrance. If you want to stay out late listening to electronic music downtown, this is the place. reviews.desc: Inspired by the aperitivo bars of Spain and Northern Italy, this little Greenpoint spot is the ideal place to drink an appletini and chat with a date.
reviews.text: let us help you make a decision Bar Americano 180 Franklin St, Brooklyn, NY 11222 If you think you’re too cool to drink an appletini, you’re wrong. No one’s too cool for an appletini. Also, the version at Bar Americano is fantastic. This little Greenpoint spot was inspired by the aperitivo bars of Spain and Northern Italy, but the menu doesn’t always stay on theme. In addition to anchovies, vermouth, and a variety of European wines, they serve a burger, a house margarita, and the aforementioned appletini (which actually tastes like apples). Bring a date, share a fried chicken sandwich, and spend an hour or two in the candlelit room that features stucco walls, brass accents, and a few leather booths. reviews.title: Bemelmans Bar - Review - Upper East Side - New York - The Infatuation
reviews.desc: Drink a stellar martini and pretend you're in an F. Scott Fitzgerald novel at Bemelmans, an iconic Upper East Side hotel bar.
reviews.text: let us help you make a decision Bemelmans Bar 35 E 76th St, New York, NY 10021 Inside the Carlyle Hotel on the Upper East Side, Bemelmans is an NYC night out that everyone should experience at least once—even if it means toughing out an hour-long line to get in. Murals by Madeline illustrator Ludwig Bemelmans decorate the walls of the piano bar, open since 1947, and the ceiling gleams with gold leaf. If you’re lucky, you might spot Bill Murray having a martini in the corner, or crashing a set. Expect to spend north of $26 for a drink. They make a stellar martini with a sidecar, and serve some of the city's finest free snack mix, which features dainty, extra-small potato chips. Neither the $10 live-music cover charge, nor an influx of influencers have dulled Bemelmans' timeless charm. We don't even mind when a corner of our neighbor's Louboutin shopping bag pokes us in the ribs.

reviews.desc: Cafe Balearica is a two-story spot in Williamsburg with a casual cocktail bar on the ground floor and a club-like space in the basement where you can dance beneath a disco ball.
reviews.text: let us help you make a decision Cafe Balearica 44 Berry St, Brooklyn, NY 11249 Considering how many bars there are in the neighborhood, you would think that Williamsburg would be stuffed with places where you can dance. Not the case. Cafe Balearica is a great option, though. This two-story spot on the corner of 11th and Berry has a ground-floor space with tropical plants, high ceilings, and a big vibrant mural in addition to a clubby downstairs room where you can dance beneath a disco ball with a bunch of people you’ve probably seen at the Williamsburg Trader Joe’s. The downstairs is only open on Fridays and Saturdays (starting at 9pm), so that’s when you should stop by if you’re looking for a scene. reviews.title: Clemente Bar - Review - Flatiron - New York - The Infatuation
reviews.desc: The best way to experience Flatiron’s Eleven Madison Park is by grabbing a drink at sister establishment Clemente Bar.
reviews.text: let us help you make a decision Clemente Bar 11 Madison Ave, New York, New York 10010 We love a celtuce tostada as much as the next person. But if we had to pick a highlight from Eleven Madison Park, it might be the tableside Manhattan cart. The plant-based fine-dining spot excels at cocktails, and you can try one without committing to a blowout dinner. Bring a date or a client, skip the $225 tasting, and choose an a la carte snack or two, like the carrot tartare or tofu dog under a blanket of shaved truffle. The vegetarian food is just as compelling as what's served downstairs, but it doesn’t have to meet the impossible expectations of a $1,000 check.

reviews.title: Elvis - Review - NOHO - New York - The Infatuation
reviews.desc: One of those sexy little wine bars where you can drink chilled red and eat an artichoke.
reviews.text: let us help you make a decision Elvis 54 Great Jones St, New York, New York 10012 From the team behind downtown darling Le Dive comes Elvis, a wine bar in a storied NoHo building that used to house Great Jones Cafe. Yes, a bust of Elvis is apparently hiding somewhere around here, but you don’t get to see it inside the bar for legal reasons. Instead, come to drink wine on a stool in front of the big window that looks out onto the cobblestone street. If Le Dive is for sitting outside and gossiping loud enough that people can hear you, Elvis is for telling someone a dirty secret without anyone hearing you at all. When you get peckish, order the artichoke with a mustardy aioli, and the sandwich with peanut butter, bacon, banana, and honey. We promise it's good. reviews.text: let us help you make a decision HiLot 102 Avenue C, New York, NY 10009 HiLot is from the team behind Joyface, an Alphabet City bar (right next door) where you can dance under a disco ball and hang out on a waterbed until 3am. But this is a different sort of place. There’s no standing room, and you have to make a reservation if you want a guaranteed seat. The space looks like a fancy living room from the 1970s, with plaid carpets, a mirrored ceiling, and fringed lamps perched on top of a winding leather couch. It’s essentially a speakeasy (complete with a doorbell you ring to get in) that isn’t hidden, and it’s a great option for when you want to go out in the East Village but don’t necessarily need to stand shoulder-to-shoulder with folks who might spill their espresso martinis on you. reviews.desc: La Caverna is a Mexican restaurant on the LES where you can eat tacos and smoke hookah in a basement built like a cave.
reviews.text: At first glance, La Caverna seems like the Rainforest Cafe offshoot no one asked for. It’s a restaurant and dance club on the Lower East Side where a door with a simple cave painting leads you to a basement with stalactites on the ceiling and walls the texture of rock bleeding purple light from the crevices. But that’s where commitment to the paleolithic theme ends. La Caverna serves some pretty solid Mexican food and margaritas in a space that just happens to be a cavernous room. At night, it turns into more of a party with music blasting out of speakers embedded in the fake rock walls and big groups ordering hookah at the bar. If that’s not your thing, come before 8pm for a fun, lowkey spot when you want to do Taco Tuesday somewhere a little different. reviews.desc: Le Dive is a busy little wine bar in a very busy part of the Lower East Side, and it's a great spot to drink, snack, and take in a scene.
reviews.text: let us help you make a decision Le Dive 37 Canal St, New York, NY 10002 Le Dive is in the middle of Dimes Square, the perennially-packed Lower East Side micro-neighborhood where fashion trends go to live fast and die young. So it should come as no surprise that this natural wine bar is kind of annoying. But that buzzy, annoying energy is part of why you come here (and visit Dimes Square in general). The space itself is fairly small, with a handful of stools and a single row of tables, but the seating-filled plaza out front has plenty of room for anyone who wants to sniff natural wine. Since “à manger” sounds chicer than “to eat,” the menu is partly in French, and it has a few snacky options like burrata, charcuterie, and some pleasantly peppery steak tartare. reviews.title: Lei is a wine-first wine bar that happens to do a great short rib - Review -  New York - The Infatuation
reviews.desc: Closet-sized Chinatown wine bar Lei pairs an extensive bottle list with creative Chinese-American small plates.
reviews.text: On the wine bar spectrum, there are places like Sauced where you can put away a bottle without eating a crumb, and spots like Sunn’s and Wildair that are really just restaurants with an overabundance of chenin blanc. Lei, in Chinatown, fits somewhere in the middle. The sliver of a wine bar is primarily a place to nerd out over riesling and German chardonnay. You can, technically, eat a full meal in the snug room with dripping candlesticks—and the small plates, with their loose Chinese inspiration, are more interesting than most—but that’s not the best way to use this place. Bring a date, stick to snacking, and focus on what’s in your glass.
